cse-1998-a-41.approach: Test each closure claim; a single counterexample kills a "for every" statement. Subsets of regular sets are not closed — any language is a subset of the regular set $\Sigma^*$.

steps.title: Finite sets are always regular
steps.body: Any finite set $\{w_1,\dots,w_m\}$ equals the regular expression $w_1+\dots+w_m$. So **A** and **C** (finite subsets of anything) are true.

steps.title: Intersection
steps.body: Regular languages are closed under intersection (product DFA), so **D** is true.

steps.title: Arbitrary subsets
steps.body: $\{0,1\}^*$ is regular, yet its subset $\{0^n1^n \mid n\ge 0\}$ is not regular (pumping lemma). So **B** is false.

answer.value: B — every subset of a regular set is regular (false)

optionAnalysis.reason: True: a finite set is regular regardless of where it came from.
False: $0^n1^n \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ is non-regular although $\{0,1\}^*$ is regular.
True: finite sets are regular.
True: regular sets are closed under intersection via the product automaton.

pitfalls: Confusing "subset" closure with closure under operations like intersection.

cse-1998-a-43.approach: All four are commutative; test associativity with a small counterexample. NAND fails, the other three are associative.

steps.title: Commutativity
steps.body: AND, OR, NAND, XOR are all symmetric in their two inputs, so each is commutative.

steps.title: Associativity of NAND
steps.body:
Take $a=0,b=1,c=1$:

$(a\uparrow b)\uparrow c=(0\uparrow1)\uparrow1=1\uparrow1=0$

$a\uparrow(b\uparrow c)=0\uparrow(1\uparrow1)=0\uparrow0=1$

$0\ne1$, so NAND is not associative.

optionAnalysis.reason: AND is both commutative and associative.
OR is both commutative and associative.
NAND is commutative but $(0\uparrow1)\uparrow1=0\ne1=0\uparrow(1\uparrow1)$.
XOR is associative (parity of three bits does not depend on grouping).

pitfalls: Treating XOR as non-associative; it is associative.
cse-1998-a-43.verification: NOR fails the same way; AND/OR/XOR verified associative via truth tables.

In the $60\times60$ square, $|X-Y|>10$ is two right triangles with legs $50$:

$$2\times\tfrac12\times50\times50=2500$$

cse-1998-a-57.approach: Track the value mod 5 while reading bits MSB first: appending bit $b$ maps remainder $r$ to $(2r+b)\bmod5$. Leading zeros keep remainder 0, so they are ignored automatically. The 5 remainders are pairwise distinguishable, so 5 states are minimum.

steps.title: Transition rule
steps.body: If the prefix read so far has value $v\equiv r\pmod5$, after bit $b$ the value is $2v+b\equiv 2r+b\pmod 5$. States $q_0..q_4$ = remainder; start = accept = $q_0$.

steps.title: Trace 1010 (= 10)
steps.body: $q_0\xrightarrow{1}q_1\xrightarrow{0}q_2\xrightarrow{1}q_0\xrightarrow{0}q_0$ — accepted, and indeed $10=2\times5$.

steps.title: Minimality
steps.body: For remainders $r\ne s$ the states are distinguishable: pick a suffix $w$ taking $r$ to 0; it takes $s$ to a different remainder since $x\mapsto 2^{|w|}x+c$ is a bijection mod 5. Hence 5 states is the minimum.

pitfalls: Adding a separate state for leading zeros — unnecessary, since $0$ keeps $q_0$ on $q_0$.

cse-1998-a-57-a.approach: IMP computes $a\to b=\overline a+b$. Write $f=x\overline y+\overline x y$ in the form $\overline a+b$: $f=g_1\to\overline{g_2}$ with $g_1=x\to y$ and $g_2=y\to x$; the negation $\overline{g_2}=g_2\to0$ needs the constant 0.

steps.title: Gate identities
steps.body: $a\to b=\overline a+b$, so $a\to0=\overline a$ and $\overline{x\to y}=x\overline y$.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body:
$g_1=x\to y=\overline x+y$

$g_2=y\to x=\overline y+x$

$g_3=g_2\to0=\overline{g_2}=\overline x\,y$

$f=g_1\to g_3=\overline{g_1}+g_3=x\overline y+\overline x y$ ✓ (4 gates)

steps.title: Why the constant 0 is needed
steps.body: IMP is 1-preserving: $1\to1=1$. Any circuit of IMP gates fed only by $x,y$ outputs 1 when $x=y=1$, but $f(1,1)=0$. So a constant-0 input is unavoidable.

cse-1998-a-57-a.verification: Truth table: $(x,y)=(0,0)$: $g_1=1,g_3=0\Rightarrow f=0$; $(0,1)$: $g_3=1\Rightarrow f=1$; $(1,0)$: $g_1=0\Rightarrow f=1$; $(1,1)$: $g_1=1,g_3=0\Rightarrow f=0$ ✓.

cse-1998-a-57-b.approach: Build a known complete set: NOT from $x\to0$ and OR from $(x\to0)\to y$. Since {NOT, OR} is functionally complete, so is IMP (with the constant 0).

steps.title: NOT gate
steps.body: $x\to0=\overline x+0=\overline x$.

steps.title: OR gate
steps.body: $(x\to0)\to y=\overline{\overline x}+y=x+y$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: {NOT, OR} is complete (AND by De Morgan: $xy=\overline{\overline x+\overline y}$), hence every Boolean function can be built from IMP gates and the constant 0.

answer.value: x→0 = x̄ (NOT); (x→0)→y = x + y (OR); {NOT, OR} is complete

pitfalls: Claiming completeness without a constant: IMP alone preserves 1, so the constant 0 is required.
cse-1998-a-57-b.verification: AND directly: $(x\to(y\to0))\to0=\overline{\overline x+\overline y}=xy$; truth table confirms all four rows.
